story.headline: Democrats won the US Senate and are projected to take the House, pushing the dollar to about a one-month low on bets of less government spending; gold jumped back above $4,000.

reads.policy: Most big central banks still lean toward higher rates, and the Bank of England is set to raise on Thursday. New Zealand’s weak jobs figures cut bets on a December hike there, and Australia’s central bank now looks done. Currencies are moving on hints about the next step, not the hikes already made.
reads.growth: The US economy keeps surprising on the strong side, but a Democratic Congress is expected to spend less, which could slow it next year. New Zealand’s job market weakened more than expected, a drag on the kiwi. The US services survey today is the next check on American strength.
reads.inflation: Fuel is still pushing prices up almost everywhere, though oil has eased from its late-October high. This morning’s euro-area figures are the week’s main inflation check, and a hot reading would firm up a December hike by the European Central Bank. Cheaper oil, if it lasts, would ease pressure on central banks across the board.
reads.risk: Asian shares fell as Democrats won the US Senate and headed for the House, with chip and AI stocks hit hardest. This time the dollar was not the safe place: money went to the franc, the yen, gold and US government bonds. Currencies tied to growth, like the Aussie and kiwi, missed out on the dollar’s fall.
reads.tot: Oil bounced a little after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said tankers hit mines near Hormuz, but it stays well below its late-October high. That leaves exporters like Canada with less support than a month ago and importers like Japan and the euro area with a smaller bill. A peace deal would widen that gap quickly.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and they are also betting against the euro and the kiwi, while real money investors bet for the euro. Their large bets on gold have been shrinking. New figures arrive Friday.
reads.fiscal: A Democratic Congress is expected to limit President Trump’s spending plans, which takes some support away from the dollar. Debt worries in France still weigh on the euro. Canada presents its federal budget on Thursday, and a big rise in borrowing would weigh on the loonie.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and strong US jobs figures have made a December hike look likely. Democratic wins in Congress may slow spending, which could ease some pressure over time.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal on high energy prices, and a busy jobs market shows the economy can take higher rates.
fed.watch: The ISM services survey at 9:00 AM CT Wednesday and Friday's October jobs report: strong figures would all but lock in a December hike.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% on October 28, its first hike since 2023, and Governor Tiff Macklem said this week that more may be needed. But the economy has stalled, so the bank says it will move carefully.
boc.priced: December: another hike slightly more likely than not.
boc.why: Energy has lifted Canadian inflation, which the bank sees near 3.5% by year-end, but growth is running well below what it expected.
boc.watch: Macklem’s speech on Thursday, Canada’s federal budget on Thursday afternoon and October jobs figures on Friday, plus oil prices.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by holding at 2.75% on October 28, and weak job figures since then have cut bets on a December hike. That leaves the kiwi with less support going into Saturday's election.
rbnz.priced: December: hike still slightly more likely than not, but less so after weak jobs data.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the 1–3% target, but unemployment has risen to its highest since 2015, which eases pressure on wages and prices.
rbnz.watch: The general election on Saturday, November 7, and any comments from the bank before its December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% on October 29, and President Christine Lagarde said a hike was discussed, pointing to December. Euro-area inflation figures out Wednesday morning will show whether that plan holds.
ecb.why: Energy costs have pushed euro-area inflation well above the 2% goal, and factory costs are rising at their fastest since May.
ecb.watch: Euro-area inflation for October at 4:00 AM CT Wednesday and ECB President Christine Lagarde's speech at noon CT Thursday.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on October 30, with one member voting to hike, and said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal. A December hike looks likely and would give the yen, now near 157.6 per dollar, more support.
boj.why: The bank judges inflation to be running at its goal, with prices rising beyond energy and the jobs market tight.
boj.watch: Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech at 10:00 AM CT Friday, Japanese wage and price figures, and any move by Tokyo to buy yen; the next decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three of nine members wanted to wait and it dropped its hint of more. Markets now expect its next move, in time, to be a cut.
rba.priced: December: no move expected; some cuts priced by the end of next year.
rba.why: Inflation has run hotter than the bank expected and will stay above its target until late 2027, but a weakening job market argues for caution.
rba.watch: Australian jobs and inflation figures before the December 8 decision, and the Chinese yuan, which the Aussie often follows.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, its first hike since 2023, and the debate is already about December. A weaker US dollar has lifted the pound ahead of the decision.
boe.priced: November: hike all but certain; December: a second hike possible.
boe.why: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, driven by energy and fuel, and factory prices are climbing faster.
boe.watch: The decision and Monetary Policy Report at 6:00 AM CT Thursday, November 5: any hint about December matters more than the hike itself.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and has said it is less ready to fight a weaker franc. Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October on fuel, which makes another cut less likely, though not a hike.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Fuel lifted Swiss inflation to its highest since late 2023, but underlying prices stayed calm, so the bank has no reason to raise rates.
snb.watch: Chairman Martin Schlegel’s speech on Thursday and the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the upper half of the board because the Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates in December and US inflation runs hot. Democratic wins in Congress, which point to less government spending, now weigh on it.

notes.policy: The Fed's next move still looks like a hike, likely in December, after strong jobs figures.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running well above the Fed's goal, mostly on fuel, though cheaper oil could start to ease it.
notes.fiscal: Democrats won the Senate and are projected to take the House, so President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which takes support from the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: growth is uneven, energy imports cost more, and France's debt worries weigh on it. A likely European Central Bank hike in December and a weaker US dollar give it some support.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank held in October and points to a hike in December, so it lags banks that are moving sooner.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth is uneven: France shrank over the summer, Italy stalled and business surveys keep missing.
notes.inflation: Prices are rising fast in Italy and France, which keeps pressure on the European Central Bank to hike.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so high oil drains money out, though prices have fallen sharply this week.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: Two of the three big rating firms now have France on negative outlook, which keeps investors wary of euro-area bonds.

GBP.summary: The pound tops the board because the Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on Thursday, November 5, inflation is high and business surveys are strong.

notes.policy: The Bank of England is expected to raise rates on Thursday, November 5, among the most likely hikes of any major bank.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been stronger than expected, with factories at their busiest in two years, even though shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, which keeps the Bank of England leaning toward hikes.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators betting heavily against the pound, so a firm Bank of England could force them to buy it back.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below other major economies' and high oil costs Japan money. It still gains when markets get nervous, as they did after the US midterm results.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rate is still far below others', though it says inflation has reached its goal, which points to a December hike.
notes.risk: The yen gains when investors look for safety, as they did when Asian shares fell on the US midterm results.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country; cheaper oil would ease that.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators holding unusually big bets on the yen, which could unwind fast if it weakens.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates, but the franc still draws money when markets get nervous.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October, mostly on fuel, but underlying prices are calm, so the Swiss National Bank still has no reason to raise rates.
notes.risk: The franc tends to gain when investors look for safety, and it was the biggest winner when shares fell on the US midterm results.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well because Australia’s rates are now the highest among major economies and it sells resources abroad. But the central bank hinted it may pause after its latest hike, and a weakening job market is a drag.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest of the major banks, but it dropped its hint of more.
notes.growth: Business surveys slipped into decline in October and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying inflation ran hotter than the bank expected and is set to stay high until late 2027.
notes.tot: Australia sells energy and resources abroad, so high prices bring money in, though oil’s sharp fall trims that.
notes.positioning: Real money investors hold some of their biggest bets against the Aussie in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well now that the Bank of Canada has started raising rates and oil brings money in. Growth is the soft spot, and cheaper oil trims its support.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and its governor says more may be needed, so a December hike is slightly more likely than not.
notes.growth: Canada's economy did not grow in July or August, well short of what the Bank of Canada expected.
notes.inflation: Producer and raw-material prices are rising fast, which keeps the Bank of Canada leaning toward more hikes.
notes.tot: Canada is a big oil exporter, so high crude prices bring money in, though oil has fallen from its late-October high on hopes of an end to the Iran war.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits in the middle of the board: New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike, and unemployment has now risen to its highest since 2015. Firm dairy prices limit the damage, and Saturday's election adds uncertainty.

notes.growth: Unemployment rose to 5.7%, the highest since 2015, and jobs fell, which weakens the case for a December rate hike.
notes.tot: Dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, have risen at three auctions in a row, bringing money into the country.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so good news could force them to buy it back.
